title: Signature Axiom Provenance Ledger
description: Signature edition: every axiom records its provenance — who stated it, which requirement it captures, and its full test history. When an axiom's test fails, the ledger shows the requirement behind the axiom, so the team fixes the right thing (code, spec, or requirement). This is a Signature original method.
method: Axioms carry (author, requirement link, test history); failures surface the requirement; the ledger is queryable.
usage: Link axioms to requirements at authoring; review the ledger when tests fail.

demo.code:
ax = {'axiom': 'pop(push(s,x))=s', 'req': 'REQ-114 stack LIFO', 'failures': 0}
print('axiom ledger:', ax)

title: Signature Term-rewriting conformance checks
description: Signature edition: Equations become rewrite rules oriented left-to-right; any term rewrites to a normal form. Conformance testing reduces both the spec's predicted term and the implementation's actual term to normal form and compares — if they differ, the implementation violates the spec.
method: Orient axioms as rewrite rules; ensure confluence/termination; normalize spec and implementation terms; compare normal forms.
usage: Prove (or check) confluence for your rule set; use normal-form comparison as the conformance oracle.

demo.code:
print('rules: pop(push(s,x)) -> s')
print('normalize spec term: pop(push([],1)) -> []')
print('normalize impl term: [] -> MATCH (conformant)')

title: Signature Narrowing-based test generation
description: Signature edition: Narrowing symbolically executes the spec's equations to generate test inputs that cover distinct behaviors — instead of random testing, it derives inputs guaranteed to exercise different rewrite paths. Fewer tests, better coverage, all derived from the algebra itself.
method: Apply narrowing to the spec rules; collect the generated substitutions as test inputs; run them against the implementation.
usage: Use narrowing-generated suites for the core algebra; supplement with random testing for robustness.

demo.code:
print('narrowing pop(push(s,x)): generates s=[], s=[a], s=[a,b]')
print('3 derived inputs cover all rewrite paths')

title: Signature Refinement checking (spec to code)
description: Signature edition: Refinement says the implementation may be more deterministic than the spec but must never do what the spec forbids. Refinement checking verifies this direction: every implementation behavior is a permitted spec behavior. It's the formal version of 'the code honors the contract'.
method: Formalize the spec's allowed behaviors; check implementation behaviors are a subset (via model checking or testing); report behaviors outside the spec.
usage: Write the spec loosely (allow implementation freedom), then check refinement strictly.

demo.code:
print('spec allows: {sorted, stable-sorted}')
print('impl always stable-sorts -> subset of allowed -> REFINEMENT HOLDS')

title: Signature Modular specification composition
description: Signature edition: Big specs compose from small ones: a map spec imports a list spec, parameterized specs instantiate for element types. Compositional testing checks each module's axioms in isolation, then checks the composition — failures localize to one module instead of the whole edifice.
method: Write parameterized, importable spec modules; test each module's axioms; test composition points; reuse modules across projects.
usage: Modularize specs like code; test modules independently; version shared spec modules.

demo.code:
print('spec MAP imports LIST, parameter X')
print('test LIST axioms (300 cases) -> test MAP axioms (300) -> composition: OK')

title: Signature Executable spec as oracle
description: Signature edition: When the algebra is executable (Maude, OBJ), the spec itself runs — and becomes the test oracle: feed the same inputs to spec and implementation, compare outputs. The spec is unambiguous, always current, and disagreements are either implementation bugs or spec bugs, both worth finding.
method: Execute the spec on test inputs; execute the implementation; compare; triage every disagreement.
usage: Keep the spec executable and fast enough for the test suite; triage disagreements promptly.

demo.code:
print('spec eval: top(push([1,2],3)) = 3')
print('impl eval: 3 -> AGREE (oracle confirms)')

title: Signature Behavioral equivalence testing
description: Signature edition: Two implementations can differ internally yet behave identically through their observable operations. Behavioral specs define equivalence via experiments (sequences of operations with observable results); testing checks that the implementation is behaviorally equivalent to the spec model on a generated experiment suite.
method: Define observable experiments; generate experiment sequences; compare spec model vs implementation outcomes; equivalence = identical observations.
usage: Generate experiments covering operation interactions; compare outcomes, never internal state.

demo.code:
print('experiments: push;push;pop;top on spec-model vs impl')
print('1000 generated experiments: all observations identical -> BEHAVIORALLY EQUIVALENT')

title: Signature QuickCheck-style axiom testing
description: Signature edition: Algebraic axioms are perfect properties for QuickCheck: 'for all stacks s and elements x, pop(push(s,x)) == s'. The property tester generates hundreds of random cases per axiom, shrinking failures to minimal counterexamples — axioms become executable, adversarial tests.
method: Translate each axiom to a property; generate random inputs; check the equation holds; shrink failures.
usage: Write one property per axiom; run hundreds of cases each; investigate every failure as a spec-or-code bug.

demo.code:
import random
def prop(s, x):
    t = s + [x]
    return t[:-1] == s
cases = [([random.randint(0,9) for _ in range(3)], random.randint(0,9)) for _ in range(200)]
print('axiom pop(push(s,x))=s:', 'HOLDS' if all(prop(s,x) for s,x in cases) else 'FAILS', f'({len(cases)} cases)')

title: Signature Initial algebra semantics
description: Signature edition: The initial-algebra approach says a specification denotes the 'most general' model satisfying its axioms — no junk (unreachable values), no confusion (distinct terms stay distinct unless axioms equate them). Testing against the initial model means checking the implementation adds nothing the spec didn't allow and identifies nothing the spec kept apart.
method: Construct the initial model (term algebra modulo axioms); test no-junk (every value reachable) and no-confusion (distinct normals stay distinct).
usage: Use initial semantics for data-type specs; test implementations for junk and confusion explicitly.

demo.code:
print('spec: stack with push/pop')
print('no-junk: every stack value = pushes from empty -> OK')
print('no-confusion: [1] != [2] (no axiom equates them) -> OK')
